extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, policymakers interested in misinformation and information integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for identifying, moderating, correcting, and preventing misinformation on social media and news platforms, with attention to public-health risks, free-speech concerns, and intervention effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of government-agency guidance for content moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media censorship policies relying on government agency-issued guidance to determine information validity have garnered criticism that such policies have the unintended effect of stifling dissent and criticism of government positions and policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should be cautious about basing removal decisions solely on government-issued guidance because this can be perceived as censorship and may stifle legitimate dissent; consider transparency and safeguards when using official guidance to assess content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature censorship of developing hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Most recently, social media companies have faced criticism over allegedly prematurely censoring the discussion of the SARS‑CoV‑2 Lab Leak Hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When content concerns unsettled or evolving scientific hypotheses, moderation policies should balance misinformation harms against the risk of suppressing legitimate scientific or journalistic inquiry; premature takedowns can provoke criticism and later regret if content is later found partially accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal for content promoting unproven medical treatments / self‑harm prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Other accusations of censorship appear to stem from attempts to prevent social media consumers from self-harm through the use of unproven COVID-19 treatments. Example: a viral video claiming hydroxychloroquine was an effective cure was taken down for violating community guidelines on spreading misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms commonly justify removals when content promotes unproven medical treatments with potential for serious harm; community guidelines may explicitly prohibit content that encourages self-harm or unsafe medical advice. Documented public-health risks and authoritative medical warnings (e.g., FDA) support such actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement under community guidelines on spreading misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The hydroxychloroquine video 'was taken down for violating community guidelines on spreading misinformation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit community guidelines that define 'spreading misinformation' enable enforcement; guidance should specify thresholds (e.g., demonstrably false medical claims that risk harm) and provide appeal/clarification mechanisms to reduce perceptions of arbitrary censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify against reputable scientific and regulatory authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: NIAID director Dr. Anthony Fauci and members of the World Health Organization (WHO) quickly discredited the video, citing larger-scale studies ... and the FDA cautioned against using it to treat COVID-19 patients following evidence of serious heart problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims by checking them against consensus positions and statements from relevant scientific bodies, peer-reviewed studies, and regulatory agencies; prioritize evidence from larger-scale studies and official safety advisories when evaluating health-related content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact‑checking and corrective presentation (e.g., related stories / truth sandwich)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research on the correction of misinformation includes techniques such as 'related stories functionality' and the 'truth sandwich' for correction of misinformation through social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction strategies should present the factual information prominently, avoid repeating the false claim more than necessary, and provide clear sourcing; design choices (placement, framing) affect effectiveness. Related-stories features and 'truth sandwich' are cited as ways to correct misinformation in-platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design corrections to avoid backfire / familiarity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies note the 'continued influence of misinformation' and test for the 'familiarity backfire effect' (i.e., that corrections can spread misinformation to new audiences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections must be crafted to minimize familiarity-based reinforcement of the false claim; use clear factual restatements and context, and consider empirical findings that simple repetition of the myth can increase familiarity. Monitor for unintended spread to new audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prebunking / psychological inoculation as preventive intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: A guide to prebunking: a promising way to inoculate against misinformation; psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively exposing audiences to refuted arguments or to the techniques used by misinformation (prebunking) can build resistance; implement educational interventions and games that rehearse recognition of manipulation tactics before exposure to false claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourced and scaled fact‑checking (wisdom of crowds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scaling up fact-checking using the wisdom of crowds; leveraging structured trusted-peer assessments to combat misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms and organizations can scale verification by aggregating judgments from many users or trusted peers; design must ensure assessor quality, prevent gaming, and combine crowd signals with expert review for reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and treating visual/AI-generated misinformation (deepfakes, cheapfakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research and guidance on deepfakes, AI-generated images, and techniques to spot them (reverse image search, digital media literacy); 'Deepfake detection by human crowds, machines, and machine-informed crowds' and advice 'AI-generated images are everywhere. Here's how to spot them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate visual content for signs of manipulation, use reverse-image and metadata checks, apply specialized detection tools, and educate users on visual literacy; proactive platform measures and research into human+machine detection improve resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information literacy education as a long‑term defense
rubrics_metrics.description: New Jersey becomes first state to mandate K‑12 students learn information literacy; library instruction can help navigate visual health misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate media and information literacy into education (K–12 and beyond) to improve people's ability to evaluate sources, verify claims, and resist misinformation over the long term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for psychological and demographic susceptibility factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Research identifies factors like analytic cognitive style, age (older Americans more vulnerable to prior exposure effects), partisanship, and other psychological drivers that affect susceptibility to misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interventions and communications with audience heterogeneity in mind: tailor strategies for age groups, partisan audiences, and cognitive styles; targeted interventions may be more effective than one-size-fits-all approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional myth‑busting resources and authoritative debunking
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO 'COVID‑19 Mythbusters' and other institutional resources are cited as tools for combating health misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplify and link to authoritative institutional myth‑busting resources (e.g., WHO, national health agencies) when correcting health-related misinformation, but remain mindful of concerns about overreliance on institutions for moderation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation of interventions (measure efficacy and effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous studies and meta-analyses cited (e.g., MIST psychometric measure, research on the efficacy/effectiveness of misinformation interventions) highlight the need to evaluate which interventions work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement evidence-based interventions and measure outcomes (e.g., belief change, sharing behavior, resilience). Use validated instruments (like MIST) and randomized or controlled designs where feasible to assess impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability in moderation decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversies around removals (e.g., New York Post Hunter Biden laptop takedown, political backlash) show the reputational risks of opaque moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should provide clear rationale, labeling, appeals processes, and transparency reporting to reduce perceptions of politically biased censorship and to retain public trust when enforcing misinformation policies.
